documents.title: What the half-turns are for
documents.source_line: ** [`rh3.html`](../rh3.html) — §9 "Why η and not ζ", theorem box at lines 634–637
header: **Source:** [`rh3.html`](../rh3.html) — §9 "Why η and not ζ", theorem box at lines 634–637

> The alternation is the analytic-continuation device. The plain zeta train exists only for σ > 1; the alternating one exists on all of σ > 0, which is where the critical strip is. Geometrically: **the reason the strip can be seen at all is that the frame turns by π per level.** This is the one axiom of the construction whose analytic content is both load-bearing and completely understood.

- "The plain zeta train" is the un-alternated Dirichlet train, convergent only for σ = Re s > 1; "the alternating one" is the half-turned train, i.e. η(s) = Σ (−1)n−1 n−s, with the phase-opposite rule a + A = 0 carrying the sign.

documents.title: The half-turned train converges on σ > 0
documents.source_line: ** [`rh3/README.md`](../rh3/README.md) — §9 "η, not ζ — and the gauge closures", lines 269–286
header: **Source:** [`rh3/README.md`](../rh3/README.md) — §9 "η, not ζ — and the gauge closures", lines 269–286

> The half-turns *are* the analytic continuation device. Un-alternated, the train diverges for σ ≤ 1: at *s* = ½ + iγ₁ the partial sums grow like `√N/|1−s|` (7.0704 predicted vs 7.0705 measured at N = 10⁴, doubling each time N quadruples). With the half-turns on, pairing level 2k−1 against 2k leaves a residue of size O(|s|·k<sup>−σ−1</sup>), summable for every σ > 0.
- The half-turns are the alternation α<sub>n</sub> = (n−1)π of §4 (α<sub>n</sub> ≡ 0 with `half = off`); the un-alternated train is the `half = off` case.

documents.title: The constraints: matched winding, and a carry-proof increment floor of ≥ ½
documents.raw_status: ** PROVED (paper argument); VERIFIED (numerical, across torsions and depths)
header: **Status:** PROVED (paper argument); VERIFIED (numerical, across torsions and depths)
> **(i) Matched winding.** Where the a-helix passes through a gear it has completed *the same number of rotations about the cone* as that gear has itself. One cumulative count, never reduced mod 2π.

> **(ii) Carry-proof monotonicity.** That count's increment carries a uniform floor — half a turn per level, at any torsion — so no small positive increase, and no residual swinging the whole way round through a carry, can interrupt it.

> Constraint (i) fixes the normalisation the sign convention left implicit. Writing W(n, t) = θ(n, t)/2π, the count is the helix's winding at depth n − 1 *and* gear n's own rotation count, and W(1, t) = 0 at every torsion. So **gear 1 never turns**: depth 0, radius 1 for every σ, rate log 1 = 0, winding 0 — the origin of all four coordinates and the construction's one fixed point. At zero torsion W(n, 0) = (n − 1)/2 exactly, so consecutive a's sit antipodally.
